strengths: First systematic formalization and benchmark for global-scale audio geolocation using natural wildlife sounds, filling a clear gap relative to the well-studied image geolocation literature.

Thorough experimental protocol: multiple paradigms (regression, classification, species-range-based, retrieval) are compared under a common evaluation framework (median error, accuracy at multiple thresholds), with a naive baseline and species-oracle upper bounds providing useful context for interpreting absolute numbers.

The proposed AG-CLIP method, which augments GeoCLIP-style retrieval with an auxiliary species-checklist prediction loss, is well-motivated by the species oracle findings and shows consistent gains over baselines and off-the-shelf soundscape mapping methods (GeoCLAP, Taxabind).

Introduction of two new resources (XCDC dawn-chorus dataset, and use of iNatSounds for geolocation) plus extensive ablations (audio encoder pretraining, location encoder choice, temporal pooling strategies, location gallery construction) support reproducibility and give the community a genuinely new benchmark and codebase.

The spatiotemporal aggregation and species-richness experiments are a valuable diagnostic, revealing an important negative result (models fail to exploit multi-species signal in dense soundscapes) that is honestly reported and analyzed rather than hidden.

The multimodal geo-forensics case study and appendix explorations (multimodal retrieval, species soundscape affinity maps) are creative, illustrate potential downstream applications, and add depth to the paper's contribution beyond a single benchmark table.
Reasonably detailed limitations and societal impact discussion, including geographic bias of the dataset and privacy considerations of geolocation technology.
weaknesses: The core empirical contribution is essentially a benchmarking exercise combining known techniques (GeoCLIP, SINR, H3 grids) with a fairly incremental auxiliary loss (AG-CLIP); the technical novelty is modest even though the problem framing is new.

Absolute performance numbers remain low in absolute terms (e.g., 17.2% region-level accuracy, city-level accuracy only 6.4%), and the gap to oracle species information (97.8% region accuracy) is very large, raising questions about whether the proposed direction (species-based reasoning) is currently practical versus simply confirming that species information would help if available.

The movie geo-forensics case study (Section 5.4) is purely qualitative with only 4 examples and no ground truth or quantitative validation of correctness, so it functions more as a speculative demonstration than rigorous evidence of the application's viability.

The species-rich XCDC results (Table 3) show that models fail to leverage species diversity as hypothesized, which undercuts a central motivating hypothesis of the paper (that species-rich recordings should improve geolocation); the paper acknowledges this but does not offer a solution, leaving a key claim unresolved.

Reliance on a single audio backbone (MobileNet-V3) pretrained specifically on iNatSounds species classification limits generalizability claims; it is unclear how well findings transfer to other architectures or non-iNaturalist-style recordings (e.g., different microphones, noise conditions).

Dataset geographic bias (skewed toward Western/Northern Hemisphere regions, per the authors' own limitation statement) may limit the generality of conclusions about global audio geolocation, and this bias is not quantitatively controlled for in the main results (e.g., stratified evaluation by region).

strengths: Formalizes an underexplored problem (global-scale audio geolocation) and situates it clearly relative to image geolocation and soundscape mapping literature.

Comprehensive empirical comparison across regression, classification, retrieval, and species-range-based approaches, with consistent metrics (median error, accuracy@threshold) borrowed sensibly from the image geolocation literature.
Introduces a new benchmark (XCDC dawn-chorus recordings) and releases a codebase/benchmark, which could be useful for follow-up work.
Extensive ablations (audio backbone pretraining, location encoder choice, temporal pooling strategies, gallery construction) that aid reproducibility and give some insight into design choices.
Interesting exploratory analyses (soundscape-species affinity maps, multimodal audio-image-text retrieval) that illustrate potential of the learned embedding space beyond the core geolocation task.
Reasonably transparent about limitations (geographic bias in iNatSounds, privacy concerns) in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The proposed method, AG-CLIP, is a fairly incremental combination of an existing framework (GeoCLIP) with an auxiliary BCE loss on SINR-predicted species checklists; the methodological novelty is limited, and the main contribution is better framed as a benchmarking/empirical study than a new technique.

The gap between the oracle species-checklist upper bound (e.g., 97.8% region accuracy with full checklist) and the actual end-to-end model (17.2% region accuracy) is enormous, suggesting the paper has not meaningfully closed the gap it motivates; the practical utility of the proposed approach remains limited.

The species-rich XCDC experiments reveal that the proposed models essentially fail to leverage multi-species information (≤5.3% region accuracy, equivalent to knowing a single species), undermining the central hypothesis that motivated much of the paper (that species diversity helps) when applied in a realistic end-to-end setting rather than with oracle information.

The Multimodal Geo-Forensics section (Sec. 5.4) is purely anecdotal, based on four hand-picked movie clips with no ground truth, quantitative evaluation, or statistical treatment; it functions more as a demo than a rigorous contribution and its claims (e.g., 'confirming the presence of modality inconsistencies') are not well substantiated.

Several appendix 'bonus' experiments (fictional-location geolocation of 'Narnia'/'Hogwarts', flag/country retrieval) are fun but scientifically unsubstantiated/anecdotal and add relatively little evidentiary value to the paper's central claims.

Significance is narrow: the work is restricted to natural/wildlife sounds and a single dataset family (iNatSounds/Xeno-Canto), which, combined with iNatSounds' acknowledged geographic bias toward the Western Northern Hemisphere, limits generalizability of conclusions to broader 'audio geolocation' as framed in the title and abstract.

No human baseline or qualitative error analysis of failure modes beyond spatial heatmaps is provided, making it hard to judge how far models are from an achievable ceiling in realistic (non-oracle) settings.

The off-the-shelf baselines (GeoCLAP, Taxabind) are compared without any adaptation/fine-tuning, which somewhat inflates the apparent superiority of the proposed method since these baselines were not designed for this exact wildlife-audio geolocation setting.

strengths: First work to formalize and systematically benchmark global-scale audio geolocation using natural/wildlife sounds, filling a clear gap relative to the mature image geolocation literature.

Thorough experimental design: compares regression, classification, retrieval, and species-oracle approaches, with careful ablations of audio encoders, location encoders, pooling strategies, and retrieval galleries (Table 2, Appendix A.7).

The species-range oracle experiments are a nice scientific contribution in their own right, clearly demonstrating the theoretical ceiling of species-based geolocation and quantifying the gap between oracle and realistic/predicted performance.
Introduces two new resources (XCDC dawn chorus dataset and benchmarking protocol on iNatSounds) that could be useful for future researchers, together with released code and benchmark.

The multimodal geo-forensics case study and additional appendix explorations (soundscape affinities, multimodal retrieval with text/images) are creative and illustrate broader applicability and interpretability of the learned representations.
Good quantitative reporting practices: mean ± std over multiple runs, multiple distance thresholds, CDF plots, and spatial error maps, which aid interpretation beyond single-point metrics.
Honest discussion of limitations (geographic bias of iNatSounds, gap between short-recording and species-rich performance, privacy/ethics of geo-forensics applications).
weaknesses: The core AG-CLIP method is an incremental modification of GeoCLIP with an auxiliary checklist-prediction loss; the ablation (Table 2b) shows this addition yields small gains (2.7% at continent level, diminishing at finer scales), raising questions about the method's real novelty and impact beyond the benchmarking contribution itself.

Species-rich recordings (XCDC) results are notably weak and arguably undercut the central hypothesis: despite true species information yielding strong results, the actual models (classification, AG-CLIP) achieve only ~2.5-5.3% region accuracy, barely better than single-species information, suggesting the proposed methods do not yet deliver real progress on the harder, more realistic species-rich setting.

Movie case studies in Sec 5.4 are purely qualitative with only four examples and no ground truth, limiting their value as scientific evidence of a 'novel application domain' beyond illustrative anecdote.

The paper relies heavily on an off-the-shelf species range model (SINR) and a single audio backbone (MobileNet-V3) for all main experiments; broader exploration of audio architectures beyond small ablations (e.g. transformer-based audio encoders trained end to end) is limited.

Geographic bias of iNatSounds (skewed toward North America/Europe) directly affects both training and evaluation, and this could inflate performance in well-represented regions while the benchmark's generalizability to underrepresented regions remains unclear.

Retrieval gallery construction (using the training set itself) could be seen as giving retrieval-based methods an advantage not available in true deployment scenarios where the location distribution is unknown; this dependency is somewhat downplayed in the main text.
